summary.text: Write an even perfect number in Euclid–Euler form \(n=2^kq\), where \(q=2^{k+1}-1\) is prime; its proper divisors are \(2^i\) for \(i\le k\) and \(2^iq\) for \(i<k\), and geometric-series sums show that each divisor is at most one plus the sum of all smaller ones. Thus induction shows that their subset sums fill every integer from \(0\) to their total, which is \(n\) by perfectness, so removing the zero sum leaves exactly \(n\) distinct sums.

full_proof.text:
Let \(D(n)\) denote the set of positive proper divisors of \(n\), and let
\[
\mathcal S(D)=\left\{\sum_{d\in E}d:E\subseteq D\right\}
\]
be the set of all subset sums of a finite set \(D\), including the empty subset, whose sum is \(0\). Thus the sequence in the statement is
\[
a(n)=|\mathcal S(D(n))|-1.
\]
The subtraction removes the value \(0\). We prove that if \(n\) is even and perfect, then
\[
\mathcal S(D(n))=\{0,1,\ldots,n\}.
\]
It will then follow immediately that \(a(n)=(n+1)-1=n\).

We divide the argument into three parts.

## 1. The form of an even perfect number

Write \(\sigma(r)\) for the sum of all positive divisors of \(r\), and write
\[
s(r)=\sum_{\substack{d\mid r\\d<r}}d
\]
for the sum of its proper divisors. Thus \(\sigma(r)=r+s(r)\). A positive integer \(n\) is perfect precisely when \(s(n)=n\), equivalently when
\[
\sigma(n)=2n.
\]

Let \(n\) be positive, even, and perfect. Extract the largest power of \(2\) dividing \(n\), writing
\[
n=2^k m,
\]
where \(m\) is odd. Since \(n\) is even, \(k\geq 1\). The numbers \(2^k\) and \(m\) are coprime. The divisor-sum function is multiplicative on coprime factors, and
\[
\sigma(2^k)=1+2+\cdots+2^k=2^{k+1}-1.
\]
Set
\[
q=2^{k+1}-1.
\]
Using perfectness, we therefore obtain
\[
q\,\sigma(m)=\sigma(2^k)\sigma(m)=\sigma(n)=2n=2^{k+1}m. \tag{1}
\]
The number \(q\) is odd, so it is coprime to \(2^{k+1}\). Equation (1) shows that \(q\mid 2^{k+1}m\), and hence \(q\mid m\). Write
\[
m=jq
\]
for some positive integer \(j\). Substituting this into (1) and cancelling the positive factor \(q\) gives
\[
\sigma(m)=2^{k+1}j=(q+1)j=qj+j=m+j.
\]
Consequently,
\[
s(m)=\sigma(m)-m=j. \tag{2}
\]

We now show that \(j=1\). Because \(k\geq1\), we have \(q=2^{k+1}-1>1\). Hence
\[
j<m=jq,
\]
so \(j\) is a proper divisor of \(m\). Also \(1\) is a proper divisor of \(m\). If \(j>1\), then \(1\) and \(j\) are distinct proper divisors, and therefore
\[
s(m)\geq 1+j>j,
\]
contrary to (2). Thus \(j=1\). It follows that \(m=q\), and (2) now says
\[
s(q)=1.
\]
Since \(q>1\), this implies that \(q\) is prime: if \(q\) had a divisor \(r\) with \(1<r<q\), then both \(1\) and \(r\) would occur among its proper divisors and its proper-divisor sum would exceed \(1\).

We have proved the needed direction of the Euclid–Euler characterization:
\[
n=2^kq,\qquad q=2^{k+1}-1\text{ prime},\qquad k\geq1. \tag{3}
\]
In particular,
\[
q+1=2^{k+1}=2\cdot 2^k,
\]
so
\[
q=2\cdot2^k-1>2^k. \tag{4}
\]

## 2. A general subset-sum covering lemma

We need the following elementary lemma.

**Covering lemma.** Let \(D\) be a finite set of nonnegative integers. Suppose that every \(d\in D\) satisfies
\[
d\leq 1+\sum_{\substack{e\in D\\e<d}}e. \tag{5}
\]
Then every integer from \(0\) through \(\sum_{e\in D}e\) is a sum of a subset of \(D\), and no subset sum lies outside that interval. Equivalently,
\[
\mathcal S(D)=\left\{0,1,\ldots,\sum_{e\in D}e\right\}. \tag{6}
\]

To prove the lemma, use induction on the size of \(D\). It is immediate for \(D=\varnothing\): its only subset sum is \(0\).

Now suppose \(D\neq\varnothing\), let \(a\) be its largest element, and put \(D'=D\setminus\{a\}\). For every \(d\in D'\), removing \(a\) does not alter the set of elements smaller than \(d\), because \(a\geq d\) and \(a\neq d\). Thus condition (5) remains true for \(D'\). By induction, if
\[
T=\sum_{e\in D'}e,
\]
then
\[
\mathcal S(D')=\{0,1,\ldots,T\}.
\]
Every subset of \(D\) either omits \(a\), in which case its sum belongs to \(\mathcal S(D')\), or contains \(a\), in which case its sum is \(a\) plus a member of \(\mathcal S(D')\). Hence
\[
\mathcal S(D)=\{0,1,\ldots,T\}\cup\{a,a+1,\ldots,a+T\}. \tag{7}
\]
Because \(a\) is maximal, all members of \(D'\) are smaller than \(a\). Applying (5) to \(a\) gives
\[
a\leq 1+\sum_{e\in D'}e=T+1.
\]
Thus the two intervals in (7) overlap or are adjacent; there is no missing integer between them. Their union is therefore
\[
\{0,1,\ldots,T+a\},
\]
which proves (6).

For later use, recall also the geometric-sum identity
\[
1+2+\cdots+2^{r-1}=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}2^j=2^r-1. \tag{8}
\]
This follows immediately by induction on \(r\).

## 3. Applying the covering lemma to the proper divisors

Let \(n=2^kq\) be as in (3), so that \(q\) is prime, \(q=2^{k+1}-1\), and \(q>2^k\).

We first explicitly identify all proper divisors of \(n\). Since \(q\) is an odd prime and is coprime to \(2\), every positive divisor of \(2^kq\) has exactly one of the forms
\[
2^i\quad(0\leq i\leq k),
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
2^iq\quad(0\leq i\leq k).
\]
The divisor \(2^kq\) in the second family is \(n\) itself and is not proper. All other displayed divisors are proper. Indeed, every \(2^i\) with \(i\leq k\) is at most \(2^k<q\leq n\), and every \(2^iq\) with \(i<k\) is strictly less than \(2^kq\). Thus
\[
D(n)=
\{2^i:0\leq i\leq k\}
\;\cup\;
\{2^iq:0\leq i<k\}. \tag{9}
\]
The two displayed families are disjoint: every member of the first is at most \(2^k\), while every member of the second is at least \(q>2^k\).

We verify condition (5) for each proper divisor \(d\). There are two cases corresponding to (9).

### Case 1: \(d=2^i\), where \(0\leq i\leq k\)

The smaller proper divisors include
\[
1,2,2^2,\ldots,2^{i-1}.
\]
(When \(i=0\), this list is empty.) Their sum is, by (8),
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}2^j=2^i-1.
\]
Therefore
\[
1+\sum_{\substack{e\in D(n)\\e<2^i}}e
\geq 1+(2^i-1)=2^i=d.
\]
So (5) holds in this case.

### Case 2: \(d=2^iq\), where \(0\leq i<k\)

Consider the following two collections of proper divisors smaller than \(d\):
\[
E_1=\{1,2,2^2,\ldots,2^k\}

a nd
\[
E_2=\{q,2q,2^2q,\ldots,2^{i-1}q\}.
\]
Here \(E_2\) is empty if \(i=0\).

Every member of \(E_1\) is smaller than \(d\): by (4), a member of \(E_1\) is at most \(2^k<q\leq2^iq=d\). Every member \(2^jq\) of \(E_2\) is smaller than \(2^iq\) because \(j<i\). All these numbers are proper divisors by (9). Moreover, \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) are disjoint because members of \(E_1\) are at most \(2^k\), whereas members of \(E_2\) are at least \(q>2^k\).

Their sums are
\[
\sum_{e\in E_1}e=1+2+\cdots+2^k=2^{k+1}-1=q
\]
and
\[
\sum_{e\in E_2}e=q(1+2+\cdots+2^{i-1})=q(2^i-1).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\sum_{e\in E_1\cup E_2}e
=q+q(2^i-1)=2^iq=d.
\]
Since \(E_1\cup E_2\) is contained in the set of proper divisors smaller than \(d\), we obtain
\[
\sum_{\substack{e\in D(n)\\e<d}}e\geq d,
\]
and hence certainly
\[
d\leq1+\sum_{\substack{e\in D(n)\\e<d}}e.
\]
Thus condition (5) also holds in the second case.

We may now apply the covering lemma to \(D(n)\). It yields
\[
\mathcal S(D(n))=
\left\{0,1,\ldots,\sum_{d\in D(n)}d\right\}.
\]
Because \(n\) is perfect, the sum of its proper divisors is exactly \(n\). Therefore
\[
\mathcal S(D(n))=\{0,1,\ldots,n\}.
\]
There are \(n+1\) distinct values in this set, including \(0\). By the definition of A193279, the value \(0\) is excluded from the count, so
\[
a(n)=|\mathcal S(D(n))|-1=(n+1)-1=n.
\]
Hence every even perfect number \(n\) satisfies \(a(n)=n\), as claimed.
